summary:
New Caledonia is a French collectivity with its own local legislature, while France retains responsibility for penal law, civil-status documents and the justice system. The protections a trans visitor would rely on therefore sit in French national law, which extends to New Caledonia, and no source in this inventory records a local ordinance narrowing them.

Nothing in the inventory criminalises trans people or same-sex relations.

Same-sex marriage has been available in New Caledonia since France's 2013 marriage-equality statute, which applies here as French law. CNN reported on 29 May 2013 on the first same-sex wedding performed under that statute in France. PinkNews reported on 26 August 2012 that the government would put its same-sex marriage and adoption bill before Parliament in October 2012, fulfilling President Hollande's campaign pledge.

Discrimination on the ground of sexual identity became prosecutable under the French Penal Code through the sexual-harassment law, which reached the Code in 2012 and enabled prosecution of discrimination and transphobic conduct as discrimination; the provision was reworded to read gender identity in 2016. Because it is French law, it governs conduct in New Caledonia.

Detention is the weakest part of the record. Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code requires trans detainees to be held according to their legal gender marker rather than their anatomy, which in practice places trans women in all-male facilities where they face assault by other detainees, according to a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018. Placement follows the identity document, not the body.

France's detention-places watchdog, the CGLPL, reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of the rights of transgender detainees across all French places of deprivation of liberty. It had received referrals concerning some forty transgender persons since 2010, and inspectors visited Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse, where eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed. The prison framework the CGLPL interprets reaches establishments in New Caledonia as French law.
tangentialFactors:
The evidence on detention comes from metropolitan France rather than from New Caledonia itself. The CGLPL's findings are national in scope, and the four prisons it inspected are mainland establishments; no source describes conditions in a New Caledonian facility.

Marriage equality arrived in New Caledonia without local legislative action, following the date of the French statute. The territory's own legislature legislates on many domestic matters, but penal law and civil status are not among them, so neither the discrimination provision nor the prison placement rule can be locally repealed or locally widened.

Protection against anti-trans violence runs through the discrimination ground in the Penal Code rather than through a distinct hate-crime statute; no source in the inventory describes a separate aggravated-offence provision for transphobic attacks, and none records how the discrimination provision has been applied here.
localsOnly:
Residents of New Caledonia hold civil-status documents issued under French law, including the marriage certificate and any change of name or gender entry recorded on it, so their personal status is administered outside the territory's own institutions.

Residents in custody are held under the same Article D248 placement rule described for France, and the CGLPL's reporting covers the framework under which they are detained; referrals concerning some forty transgender persons have reached the watchdog since 2010.

Prosecution of discrimination on the ground of gender identity, as reworded in 2016, proceeds under the French Penal Code, which places handling of such complaints within the French justice system that extends to New Caledonia.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no New Caledonia-specific enforcement record: no prosecution, conviction, sentencing outcome or police-incident data concerning trans people is sourced for the territory, so the application of the French Penal Code provision here remains unresolved.

Nothing in the inventory addresses entry or visa requirements, border screening that could disclose a visitor's trans status, or the rules for changing a gender marker on a passport or identity document used for travel. These remain not sourced rather than known to be permissive or restrictive.

No source covers access to gender-affirming healthcare, facility access such as bathrooms and changing rooms, or local hate-crime sentencing practice in New Caledonia.

The inventory does not establish whether the CGLPL conducts inspections in New Caledonia or which establishments, if any, operate there; the specific prisons named in its 2021 opinion are metropolitan French facilities.
